utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Good morning, Madam Registrar, would you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that all the accused are here. All Defence teams are present, minus Mr. Bourgon on the Nikolic team. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Soljan. I take it there are no preliminaries. We just wish to make a statement. We have seen your Prosecution submission regarding proposed exhibits for Witness 47, which arrives in the wake of the debate, discussions we had yesterday at the end of the sitting. Mr. McCloskey, the Trial Chamber wishes to express its gratitude for the way to proceed that you have chosen. Thank you. There is a Prosecution motion requesting protective measures for another witness that I will come to during -- just after this witness finishes her testimony. In the meantime, if you could kindly prepare yourself to give us feedback whether oppose, object to such protective measures. You will let us know. All right. Madam -- yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Before this hearing, we consulted the other Defence teams and we have no objections for the protective measures for our next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I think we can hand down a brief oral decision here and now. The Trial Chamber seized with a Prosecution motion requesting protective measures for Witness 36 filed on the 5th of February. There being no objection on the part of the Defence teams, grants the motion allowing pseudonym and face distortion for the -- for Witness number 36. All right. Madam Palic, good morning to you, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I explained yesterday what's going to happen. Ms. Soljan is going to ask you a few questions and then I'll pass you on to the Defence teams. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Palic. How are you? Could you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is Esma Palic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 21st of March, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Zepa, and I lived my -- the first 15 years of my life in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Are you a Bosnian Muslim, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you met your husband while you were both studying at Sarajevo at the university; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your husband wasp Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And by July 1995, he was a colonel in the BiH army and the commander of the 285th Partisan Brigade which was responsible for the Zepa enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the partisan brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because -- yes, was it the 285th Partisan Brigade or just the partisan brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no partisan brigades in this war. He was the commander of the 285th Light Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. And prior to the war, your husband had been an engineer by trade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Palic, I'm going to take you back to Zepa in the early 1990s. You moved to Zepa in 1992 and stayed there until 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's partially true. I did not move until -- in fact, before the war I lived in Sarajevo. On the 29th of March, I went to Zepa to visit my parents and I stayed there because I couldn't go back. Because on the 4th of April, Zepa -- that was the Feast of Bajram which was why I went to see my parents, Zepa was blocked on that date and nobody could get out. I stayed there until the very end, until the deportation of the people from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And while you were in Zepa in 1992 through July 1995, where were you living exactly? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in my parents' house, except for the time that I spent living in the caves in the woods. So I lived in my parents' house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And where in the town of Zepa was your parents' house located?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic make-up of Zepa during March -- between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Muslims there with the exception of two teachers, who were of Serb ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And were all the people who were living in Zepa between 1992 and 1995 locals?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until 1992 they were locals, with the exception of the people who came there to work, but most of these people left when they felt that the war was near. But during the war, in 1992, one-third of the population was locals and two-thirds were refugees from the towns and villages around it. They were forced to leave their homes, their towns and villages early in 1992 by the Serbian army. Those were people from Visegrad, Rogatica, Han Pijesak, Suka, Vlasenica, and all those villages in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And by July 1995, approximately, how many people were living in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning in 1992, I really can't give you an exact figure. But if you had 5.000 locals, people were saying that there were 15.000 people living in Zepa. But in 1992, there were three offensives launched against Zepa. Zepa was in danger of falling into enemy hands, and many people who came from the outside had no more reason to stay in Zepa anymore. Many of them left in the direction of Srebrenica because Srebrenica was a corridor leading towards Tuzla. Quite a few people tried to move through the woods, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, to go to Kladanj. So the exact number of people who left, I can't give you the exact figure. I know that at the very end in 1995 there were over 8.000 people living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Palic, had there been shelling in Zepa throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was terrible. The shelling was terrible, particularly in 1992, as I already said. In 1992, there were two offensives launched against Zepa; one was in July when Zepa was shelled by tanks, mortars, and there were air strikes over an extended period of time in June, July, August, September, October; and then after that period the shelling continued, but there were no more air strikes. And the situation persisted until May 1993, when Zepa was declared a protected area and the shelling stopped until March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And as of March 1995, did the frequency of shelling change?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you compare it to the previous period when there was no shelling, in March the shells started falling again on the fringe areas, not too many, maybe one or two would fall at different ends of the town. But in June already, before the occupation of the enclaves began, that's when the shelling started in earnest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which parts of Zepa were being shelled the most, starting with March 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about March, the shells hit the fringe areas, the outskirts, uninhabited areas, wooded areas. I know that a shell hit an inhabited area and people immediately went to a nearby UNPROFOR check-point and reported that. But when the shelling started in June, the shells hit the inhabited areas, a lot of shells hit the town centre, and all the other areas that were inhabited.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And during this time of increased shelling, were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And were those civilian or military personnel?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the shelling starting in June. Can you describe, did the frequency of shelling change again at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July, the shelling was more intense than in the previous period; May, April, March. But when Srebrenica fell and when an offensive was launched against Zepa, then this can't be described as shelling at all. This was complete chaos. Shells were falling all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And during this increased shelling attack on Zepa, did you have a chance to hear General Mladic or someone purporting to be General Mladic over loud-speakers?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Srebrenica fell, when chaos reined in Zepa - because we knew we were the next on the line, and the intense shelling was a very clear sign of what was in store for us - the army surrounded Zepa. A few days after the fall of Srebrenica, maybe two or three days, I heard -- I had the opportunity to hear. One day I was on the balcony of my house, and I dared to go out. It was a daring thing to do, but I just couldn't stand being in the shelter anymore. I heard this voice. I heard this voice from the -- the rocky hills that were to the northwest of my house, that's an area called Borovacke Stijene. There were Serb army positions there, and we could hear a voice from there or I could hear a voice from there saying, "The people of Zepa, this is Ratko Mladic speaking to you. You cannot stay in Zepa. Take white flags and move to Brezova Ravan where buses are awaiting you to take you to the territory controlled by Alija Izetbegovic. Don't listen to crazy Avdo. You are his hostages. He will take you to your deaths." And several times during the day he repeated this message, calling on us to surrender, talking about the white flags. And I will never forget the phrase, what he said about listening to crazy Avdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what was your reaction to this message, if any?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not a pleasant thing to hear, because this was my husband. I was not in fear only for my own life. At that moment the most difficult thing for me was the situation with my husband. But I and many other people from Zepa, we knew that what Avdo was saying was the only thing to do. I was very frightened, but I had to get myself under control, and I had to wait, wait for whatever would happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were you able to observe how other inhabitants of Zepa were reacting to these messages coming from the mountain?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were restless. Some people would come to our house. They knew that every time there was a crisis in Zepa, people would go to the commander to ask him what to do. Avdo would come home from the headquarters and I asked him what's going on. And I knew that there were meetings going on in the municipality and the headquarters in Zepa, that people were very much frightened. Some were asking, "Should we surrender?" Others were saying, "Avdo, tell us, because we will do whatever you tell us because you know best." And then the decision was made, Avdo proposed it, and the people accepted it, that we should put up a defence because if we surrendered we would end up like the people from Srebrenica. That was a certainty. I know that at that time Avdo was in great torment. He wanted to restore peace to the people. He wanted to calm them down because if somebody is telling you you are the victims of somebody who is your own, then of course tensions occur, people start to doubt. But from the previous years, people learned that they could trust Avdo, and Avdo immediately went to UNPROFOR and asked for their assistance to protect the people of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a few more questions about the shelling that was taking place during this time. You had mentioned that there were civilian casualties. Do you know the number of these casualties during the increased days of shelling in July?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really don't know. But I know people were dying, civilians were dying. I don't know the exact figure simply because I found myself in a state, peculiar state, and I really just was concerned with my own problems and I didn't pay much attention to the -- how many people died. I know that a neighbour of mine was killed. That's what I know. I know that people were being killed all over Zepa. I know about a boy who was fleeing into the woods. He was mentally retarded, and he was killed as he was fleeing into the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, your own house was shelled during this time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was done on purpose. While Simon Dudnik, the UNPROFOR commander, was still in Zepa, he was captured by Mladic a couple of days later, at least that was the report. And he remained there while Mladic's headquarters were being established. He was in a way a kind of a liaison between the civilian authorities in Zepa and Avdo, and Mladic's forces that were positioned at Boksanica hill dominating Zepa. I remember that know one day Dudnik came to our house, and he was talking to Avdo on the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I wanted to get your details on the actual shelling if I could, please. Could you tell us when this took place?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house where I lived was shelled. It may have been the 17th or the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you describe exactly how it happened; what happened, how many shells hit the home, who was in the house at the time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a shelter in the house. It was a small shelter used by me and the babies. My mother and my sister were there. We were in the shelter because there was non-stop shelling. My baby, who was less than four months old at the time, was crying. I left the shelter, I went into the living room, and I tried to calm her down. My sister went out at the same moment, and we may have been there a minute or two. A shell hit the wall of the house, and the -- there was this huge, detonation. At the entrance door, I could feel the detonation there, and we went back into the shelter and five shells hit the house. The first shell hit the wall of the living room, which was where my sister, my baby, and I were at the time. The second shell hit the part of the wall where the shelter was, and I could hear the logs that were stacked there by this wall, I could hear them just tumble down. The third shell hit the second floor. The fourth shell, again, hit the second floor, right next to the previous one, and the fifth one hit the roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: This wasn't the first time your home had been shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: When was the first time your house was shelled, please?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time it was shelled was in December 1992. The second time was the 8th of March, 1993, and that's when it sustained some severe damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, once your house was shelled in July 1995, could you continue living in it?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We couldn't continue living in it. We were in the shelter, and we were suffocating on the dust that was coming into the shelter. We could see the smoke from our shelter. You could see when we got out. We knew we had to get out, but we tried to pick the right moment for it. We agreed I would get out with the one baby, and my mother would get out with the other baby; and when I got out in the corridor, everything was -- everything was strewn around outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, where did you end up living after that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to the outside shelter and we waited for nightfall; and then late at night, I took the babies and Avdo came. He was very, very scared for us, and we went to a village, Stitkov Dol, which was a little bit sheltered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how far away was this location from the centre of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half an hour on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, why did you choose this location?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of the terrain was such that it was more sheltered than the down-town area. That was its geographic location. In addition to that, this was the place to which we escaped from 1992 onwards on our way to the Zepa mount; and from there, we moved on through forests in emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, were there other people from your neighbourhood who were doing the same thing as you and moving towards Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody from the down-town area moved towards Stitkov Dol. From other settlements, which were on the left from the centre, there was an unwritten rule during the war that the majority of the civilians, majority of families followed the route taken by Avdo's family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how many people were there with you, moving towards Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And who were these people? What was the composition of men versus women and children, elderly?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Women, children, some elderly people, but mostly women, children, older women, and some older men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Stitkov Dol, was this area big enough to accommodate all the people who were arriving?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is but ten houses in that village, and maybe some ten outbuildings. People were out in the meadows. It was quite natural to sleep in meadows. The meadows were full of people, so were backyards and front yards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Was the shelling continuing as you were moving towards Stitkov Dol and while you were in Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as we were leaving, I don't remember that there was any shelling then, even though it was night-time, and sometimes they shelled at night as well. I don't remember that we had to take shelter. As for Stitkov Dol, where the people were, the shells did land on the other side of the hill, but none of the shells landed directly on the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at this location?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of July, at night, late, it could have been 2.00 a.m., we moved towards the mountain, because Brezova Ravan had fallen and that was one of the critical points in the defence of Zepa, critical locations. And there was a risk of the Serbian army entering Zepa. The agreement on civilians had not been reached yet. So at 2.00 a.m., we set out towards the mountain; and when we arrived, it was already daylight on the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And that morning you then received word that women, children, and elderly were going to be moved out of Zepa. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received information to go back. Before we set out, I knew that there were negotiations on the surrender of Zepa, surrender of the army, evacuation of civilians. Mladic was dissatisfied with the development of events. He kept seeking that Avdo come to negotiations and Avdo didn't want that. He was waiting for an agreement to be reached at a higher level in Sarajevo. Given that the situation was awful, I received information that if no word is received from Sarajevo, Avdo would go to negotiations; and when we were told on the 24th to go back, I knew that Avdo had participated in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what did you do next, once you found out that you were supposed to be moving out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I found out that we were to be moved out of Zepa, is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: When word came to you on the 24th while you were moving away from the centre of Zepa with other people, what did you all do next?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we went back from the mountain to the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you please describe for the Court what you observed once you arrived back in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very much afraid for my husband's fate. He had accepted to meet with the people who had threatened him throughout the war. There were buses lined up in the centre of Zepa. A huge crowd of people was moving. Near a bar, I saw some Serbian soldiers and my husband stood there with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And who were -- you said there were masses of people. Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were women, children, the elderly; mostly women and children, elderly women, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what did they look like at that moment?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrible. It's hard to describe it. At that point in time, they looked normal to me because that's how all of us looked. They looked terrified, petrified, desolate. They had lost members of their family. They were worried about their loved ones who were on the front. It was an awful situation in which nobody knew where they were going, why. The buses were there, but it gave us no reassurance to believe that we would survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what happened next? Did you board one of the buses in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in that group of people in that crowd. As I saw Avdo standing there, I moved towards him. He saw me and approached me, and he said to me, "Don't you worry." He tried to console me. He looked at the children. He said something that really scared me at that moment. He said that he had negotiated, or rather that Zdravko Tolimir was there. He pointed him out to me; I saw him. He said that he had reached an agreement with him. Given that Avdo didn't believe that the evacuation was safe, Tolimir told him to get with him into his car, to sit on the back seat, and for Avdo to keep his pistol; and that if he found anything suspicious, he could fire directly into his head and that they would be at the head of the column of civilians. I was afraid. I told him not to trust Tolimir, that it was sheer madness, that it was better for all of us to die there rather than for him to do that. This is what he told me: He knew how he felt, but what he said to me was that the civilians must be saved. So I got on the bus; I got on the bus number two. I know that I sat near the front door; I was on the second seat. I had my older daughter in my arms, and my younger daughter was with my sister. I kept looking for Avdo, and at 7.00 we set out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: How many -- do you recall how many buses there were?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how full was the bus you were in, and who was inside it?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus was full. All of the seats were taken. There were people who sat out -- who sat closer to the front. These are older-type buses, which have a -- an older-type engine hood. My mother, who was quite old at the time, sat closer to the front on the floor of the bus. And at the very back of the bus, there was one long seat, and I remember that there were people sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you had just said you had left at 7.00. You said you set out at 7.00. Do you know whether the convoy you were in was the first convoy to leave Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first convoy left somewhat earlier. This was the convoy with the wounded and the sick, and it went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how did you know this?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard. I heard that, even Avdo told me that. I know some of the wounded who were on that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And as you were leaving, were you told by anybody where your convoy, where your bus was going?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew. I didn't know -- I don't know how I knew, but I knew that we were going to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you get to speak to your husband any time between boarding the bus in Zepa and arriving at your final destination?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Somewhere between Rogatica and Sokolac, the buses stopped again. So the first time they stopped was by the hotel in Borike, and this is where I suffered a panic attack that I never really recovered from. The second time the buses stopped I saw Avdo. It was already dark; the lights were on. He came out and I was really scared wondering why he came out and why he was outside, but he came to my bus. He approached the children and then the two of us sat on the steps by the door and talked there until we disembarked in Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were you able to observe his demeanour at the time? How did he appear to you?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo, as a rule, was always calm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Palic. Do you need a short break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If at any time you need a short break, please don't hesitate. Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If you can continue just telling us about his demeanour, how he appeared to you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo was always very calm, but I could feel that he was fully aware of just how critical the situation was. I could also feel that he was quite resolute in bringing this to an end. He said to me, "Esma, I will get this done, whatever happens to me."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you know what he meant by, "I will get this done, whatever happens to me?"

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had decided to save the people of Zepa. He was quite resolute about it. In addition to that, he was fully aware that he himself was a victim and that his role would not be forgiven. They will not forgive him his role.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you then please describe what happened once you reached your final destination in the buses? When did you reach it, first of all?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We travelled for a very long time. I was pleased about that because I was with Avdo, but at the same time I knew that we were not going to the lands end. I saw that it was near 4.00 when we parted. The buses stopped, we were on the road, and to the right there were some wooden shacks. We came out and we were told that from there on we had to go on foot. Avdo and I said good-bye to each other. He said to me to move in the middle. I set out; I didn't want to turn and look back. I know that we crossed a stream. I had two babies and it was terrible. All of us were completely exhausted. But in addition to two babies, the greatest problem was my old mother, who had to be carried. And we were pulling her on a branch, on a tree branch. People were quite helpful; they offered to help me. But everybody had their own things to carry, and I had forgotten my luggage on the bus because I was so stressed out. We walked for a very long time. I know that we arrived at 9.00 at this location where there was a unit waiting for us, some Pakistani unit. They offered some refreshments. I kept wondering how Avdo was going to return to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, had you wanted to leave Zepa on the 24th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not under those circumstances, no. In reality I am really not a benchmark for you, because Zepa was not my birth town. Zepa was a place to which I always gladly travelled, where my parents lived, my relatives lived, but I didn't actually live in Zepa. Nobody wanted to leave Zepa at that time, especially not in such a humiliating way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you feel as though you had any choice?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two options: One was to leave Zepa under very cruel and humiliating circumstances; the other option was to remain and then either be killed or be subjected to suffering. There were no other options.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, have you seen or heard from your husband since that last conversation upon getting off the bus?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him again; however, on the 25th, on the 24th, on the 26th, I was in Visoko. Actually, on the 25th in the morning, we found ourselves in Kladanj; and on the 26th, I found myself in Visoko. A man came who knew my brother, and he told me that Avdo had established a connection via ham operators and wanted them to tell me that he had arrived in Zepa alive. He knew that I was worried about that; I was worried about him going back with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And have you heard from your husband ever since then?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then on the 28th -- Avdo was captured on the 27th, and I heard on the 28th that he had been captured. That's what I heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you have never seen him since; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. However, he was seen by witnesses in various clandestine prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, Ms. Palic, can you describe for us what the impact of all this has had on you and your family?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the expulsion, after the deportation from Zepa, my life was simply ruined. I arrived in that territory exhausted, both in a mental and physical sense. That was the territory under the control of Alija Izetbegovic, and I had nothing but two babies. My husband was captured. I had to look for him, beg that he be released. I knew that he was alive. For years, I waged a crusade for him to be released. In July, it's going to be 12 years since his capture, and I actually don't know what happened to him. So what can I tell you about the impact on our lives? All I can tell you is that I live in darkness, in constant suffering, with two children who need a healthy mother, after all. I live a life that was determined by Mladic, not a life that I chose for myself. Mladic decided to chase me out, Mladic captured my husband, Mladic ensured that I be left by myself at the age of 28, with two children. This was not my choice. This was not the life I chose for myself. I don't think I need to speak about the effects any longer. And could we have a break now, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break. Or as long as necessary. Victims and witnesses unit will coordinate and let us know, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Ms. Palic, we are going to proceed. Any time you need a break, please let us know. Who is going first? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Palic. I understand that you spent the entire war in Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me your husband, as the commander of the brigade, and the people from the brigade, do you know whether they were manning the front lines facing the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this period while you were in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the United Nations arrived in Zepa, yes, they were. And at the time when Mladic's forces attacked Zepa in 1995, when UNPROFOR refused to protect Zepa, that's when they went back to the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was when Zepa was shelled, I assume?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, your husband and the other members of this unit, while they were not at the front-lines, when they rested, they did so in their own homes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there no building in Zepa where they could stay, sleep, or take their meals while they were not at the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if any such building existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours. We have no questions for Mrs. Palic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nor do we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, I do have a number of questions for you, and could I begin by acknowledging, I will do this in the form of a question: You have spent considerable energy over the last ten years bringing to public attention the plight of your husband, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not ten years, almost 12 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you've done that with great tenacity, and to some real effect, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. All that I have now is still uncertain. If I may say something about the effect of one having a decision of the human rights centre on the paper and if you have to knock on every door, the authorities in Republika Srpska, the authorities in Sarajevo, the international community, to be more specific the OHR, and to demand that this decision by the human rights centre be implemented, and everything that is contained there, all the witnesses who are quoted there, this is the product of my work. And for four years, I have had nothing on the basis of that decision; and then I launched a suit before the Constitutional Court, because this decision had not been implemented. And I get a decision of this court and then a commission is set up, and this commission is working really hard to cover up all the information that I found out that I verified. They promised me that they would find my husband's body. They say, "Yes, he was killed." They gave me the name of my -- he gave me the name of his killer. But how can I know that my husband is really dead if I can't see his bones? And I filed a legal suit before the human rights court in Strasbourg. As you said yourself, I really spent a lot of energy, to prove and to bring to the public attention the fact that my husband was arrested at the UN base, that he was held in secret prisons, that he was mistreated and treated roughly, that he was never protected by the people who were immediate subordinates of Mladic. And I get these reports that he was killed and his head was chopped off with a machete, yet I have nothing to see. How -- how then am I to believe that he is dead and that he is not alive somewhere, unless I can see his bones, unless I can see his killer brought before a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I may return to that subject at the end of my questions, but I'd like now, if I may, to take you back to the beginning of the evidence you gave this morning. And you mentioned that in the enclave the population was exclusively Bosniak, save for the fact that there were two Serb teachers. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps we could have put up on the screen a document that, in fact, this Trial Chamber began looking at yesterday, which is 6D27.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's page 4 that I'm going do want you to look at. If I may, Ms. Palic, just remind the learned Judges that this was the document that describes an intelligence report from various sources. And, Madam, I'm going to show you a number of documents, some of which have not been translated. Page 4, please. And you are going to have to help me, if you would, because I'm afraid I do not read B/C/S, and so I'm going to invite you to read certain portions very slowly. Now, this is the paragraph, the third one down, that begins with the word, "Medju. " Could you read that paragraph consisting of three lines, slowly, so that the interpreters can interpret it into English and French. Aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Among the school teachers in Zepa, there are two women of Serb ethnic background. Teacher Jelenka Cesko, married to Sarija Cesko, and retired teacher Rosa" and I will now add her last name; it's Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you can confirm that the information that's contained on this piece of paper within in this report is correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have just read is correct, but I don't know about the rest because I didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Don't worry, Madam. I'm not asking you about the rest of the document, just that small portion. Thank you. We can move on to another topic, if we may. The next thing I would like to ask you about is this: You told the Trial Chamber earlier that shelling stopped in May of 1993 in the Zepa area. And it's right, isn't it, that the reason the shelling stopped was it was at that point in time that Zepa became an enclave protected by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That what is probably the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm going to invite you to have a look at 6D31. Here we have the opposite problem. This is a document that's in English, certainly I think English only. So I will have to do the work here and read out the relevant passage, and I would like you to have a look at Article 3 of this. This is the agreement signed between Mladic, General Halilovic, General Morillon on the 8th of May of 1993, turning both Srebrenica and Zepa into enclaves. And we can see the document in front of us, Article 3, that it says, "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit, hand over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives, and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR;" and then it deals with how that should be done and when that should be done, which we don't need to go into in any detail. What is your knowledge of efforts by your husband and others to obtain weapons in late 1994, early 1995, in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. In 1994, the weapons were not needed. Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will in a moment, but let me rephrase the question, if I may. We can see from the agreement that Zepa was meant to be a demilitarised zone. In your estimation, and you were there, did it remain a demilitarised zone prior to the resumption of shelling in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zepa remained a demilitarised zone up until the moment when UNPROFOR told Avdo that they could not defend Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they returned the weapons that had been kept by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was that, please?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- in fact, Srebrenica had already fallen. It was at the time when Mladic's forces started amassing around Zepa. Avdo first demanded protection from the United Nations, or rather the UNPROFOR troops in Zepa. He negotiated; he talked all the time. I know that Dudnik went to Boksanica to meet with Kusic, he was a local commander, to ask that the shelling of Zepa stop. But when the events in Srebrenica took place and we received a notice that Srebrenica had fallen, this is something that should not have happened if Srebrenica was a protected area, a UN-protected area, yet the United Nations did not protect it. Avdo knew right away that we faced the same fate and he asked them how do you intend to defend us, and it was clear that a small UN unit, the battalion stationed in Zepa could not defend it. That's when they said, "Here are your weapons. You go and defend yourselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was July of 1995, you were just describing events?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, there had been no effort on the part of the Muslim population of the Zepa enclave to rearm prior to that time. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't understand your question. What do you mean to arm itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, to take possession of any type of military armament; guns, artillery, grenades, anything whatsoever, ammunition. That's what I mean?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no such efforts, and as far as I know there was no need for it because we were in a protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 5D7, please? This document, Your Honour, has been translated. I'm in the Court's hands as to whether the Chamber would like a split screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's in the system, I think, yes. Okay. We have it already in the English language on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Madam, this is a document that we can see if we go to the bottom of the document, in fact the second page emanates - yes, the bottom of that page, thank you. The English is in two pages - from Brigadier General Hadzihasanovic. And if we to the top of the document, we see it's dated the 7th of February, 1995. We see in the right-hand corner that among the people it was sent to, was your husband at the 1st Zepa Brigade. And it details a delivery of arms to a heli-port on the following day, and number 4 specifically says, "Along with this team, Ismet Ljeskovica is going from Zepa to have him prepare for the trip." And if we scroll down a little bit, please, we see a description of various armaments and where they are intended; so 100 pieces of 7.62 millimetre automatic rifles to Zepa for example, mortars and shells, bullets, kitchen salt and some cigarettes. Did you have any knowledge of this at the time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, salt, if they're talking about salt, salt was a legendry beast. I did not see a single grain of salt throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Come now, Mrs. Palic. I think you know I'm not asking about the salt. I'm asking about the arms.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, not for the arms. And I didn't know about salt either. But the salt, I immediately saw this and that's because if you have to live throughout the war without a single grain of salt, this is something quite special, and that's why it tends to stick in your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I was being facetious, I apologise. But let me ask you a question. This Mr. Ismet Ljeskovica that we see referred to in item 4 --

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wanted to get to, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard this name ever, and I was not supposed to know the first names of people. But I couldn't now recall anyone having this last name, even among the people who had arrived in Zepa who were not originally from Zepa. So this -- this last name is completely unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I could show you a number of other similar documents from around the same period; one dated the 20th of February, another dated the 4th of March, for example, both addressed to your husband, from General Hadzihasanovic, dealing with the delivery of arms. You can confirm that you have no knowledge of that whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You didn't see men, other than the UNPROFOR soldiers, with arms within the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific when? When? Before the attack on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Specifically, I'm talking about before March of 1995 when you assert that the shelling resumed after a lull of almost two years.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of your husband organising raids outside of the enclave; in other words, organised from within the enclave, attacking Serb positions outside of the enclave, late 1994, early 1995, prior to the resumption of the shelling? Any knowledge of that at all?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I can tell you is that my husband had a defence strategy, not an attack strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would the witness be shown 6D26, please. Again, Your Honour, this is a document the Trial Chamber has seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, though we don't have a translation of this, this has been read to the Court on a previous occasion, so you can just read it to yourself, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will summarise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I know you think too highly of the Trial Chamber, but we can't remember the corresponding English translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This document indicates, does it not, Mrs. Palic, that on the 12th of December of 1994, there was some sort of raid purportedly organised by your husband from within the enclave to a place called Laze-Mislovo, and it indicates that your husband's unit suffered no losses or injuries but five Serbs, including one officer, was killed and it was some form of sabotage action. Is this a fair summary of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you accept my summary, Madam, of what the document purports to say?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading this document, but I have to tell you this is not something that I have heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does it shock you? Let me explain what I mean by that. You had absolutely no idea that your husband was involved in that sort of activity at that time? That's what I mean by, "Does it shock you?"

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even believe that this is actually true. You presented this here, and I have to tell you that I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. You have described the situation in the enclave as desperate, and now I am talking about the period from May to July of 1995. And you talked about that earlier this morning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Presumably, money was in very short supply?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no money at all, at least I didn't have any. Some people may have had some, but we didn't. And this was a normal situation. We just learned to get by without money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge of the state of the finances of the Zepa Brigade at that time, as I say, shortly before the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Zepa Brigade made some sort of loan to your husband in order to cover his desperate financial situation?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D32, please? This again, Your Honour, I regret to say has not been translated. Now, take it from me, we could go to the second page, but this is a document that emanates from Commander General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question before we look at this --

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll down? Could you please scroll down so that can I see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed. Up a bit, please. Up a bit.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen a document in this form before? This is some sort, as I understand, encrypted computer document. Did you see documents like that around your home at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. But it is my guess that this is, in fact, in light of the amount mentioned here, in 1993, when Zepa was declared a protected area, a UN-protected area, a delegation from Zepa, including Avdo, flew to Sarajevo by helicopter with approval of the Serb side. There was a congress of some sort. I don't know what it was. And on that occasion, in light of the situation in Zepa, Avdo received some funds that he was to distribute to the troops. Five thousand marks, and that's the amount mentioned here, was requested by Avdo as a loan to assist his sister and family -- and his family living in Hrasanica just outside Sarajevo. And since he never got any document to that effect, I know that he brought the money back in Sarajevo; and when he got back, the delegation -- he was not the only one there. That was the money meant to assist the troops - there were some cigarettes, too - and to assist the families who did not have any homes and who did not have anyone to provide for them, so this was to get them housing. And Avdo wanted to get some kind of a receipt for the 5.000 marks that he took to give to his sister who was in a desperate situation, but that's not what is said in this document. That's -- that doesn't reflect the situation because the -- the receipt was not dated the 2nd of July, because he received a receipt right away. And I have to say that he distributed the money that he got to the troops. I know that each soldier got 100 marks and he himself got 100 marks, and the rest was earmarked for building wooden houses or sheds for the families who did not have any accommodation, who did not have anyone to provide for them, and who were really in a desperate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't stop you because, apart from anything else, if I can avoid it, I don't stop a witness in the middle of their answer. But as I understand what you have just said, you are referring to 1993. This document refers to 1995, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the date confuses me because this was in 1993, so I'm confused a bit by the date. So why would Avdo need 5.000 marks? I don't think that the money actually existed. Avdo didn't need the money. The only logical explanation or reasoning, which I don't have to express, but I will, is that Avdo requested that again, believing his fate to be desperate, that he was in Mladic's hands, and that he needed something to prove that his family would return what he had received earlier. So that I wouldn't have any problems later on. So that would be the only logical explanation. So this date, the 2nd of July, is confusing to me because this happened in 1993. And this is something that Delic knew about, as did other members of the War Presidency in Zepa. When his sister arrived and told them about how and where she lived, he asked for money to help his sister and that he would pay the money back. And they said, "You certainly deserve for us to help your family," and he said, "No, no, no. I will pay this money back." And this is why they drafted this document confirming that, that he would pay the money back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, I don't want to belabor the point, but could I just invite you to read number 2 on the screen in front of you, which I want to then ask you a question about.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aloud --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or to myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Payment pursuant to this decision shall be made through the treasury of the Light Zepa Brigade from the funds received by the treasury of this staff for the operating needs of the said unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you give any explanation as to how the Light Zepa Brigade could afford 5.000 Deutsch marks in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By this time, July of 1995, are you able to say how many men your husband had under his command?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many, perhaps a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to suggest that he had about 1200 men under his command; and then after the fall of Srebrenica, a further 700 were at his disposal as well. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what am I supposed to say? There were definitely 1.000 men; and after the fall of Srebrenica, I don't know how many people came, definitely 500. Many of them were wounded and ended up in a hospital. Now, as to whether all of them were at his disposal, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you accept this proposition, which I could put up on the screen in front of you in English. It comes from a report that this Chamber has heard a lot of called the NIOD record, which for your information was a report commissioned by the Dutch government into the events surrounding the fall, particularly of Srebrenica, but also of Zepa. The proposition is as follows: "On the 13th of July, the Bosnian Serbs tried to persuade the Bosnian Muslims to lay down their weapons" - this is in Zepa, I should hastily add - "after which the population could choose to stay or leave." No answer was given, and I quote here to make it clear, "It was the Bosnian Muslims who wanted to fight." What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is hypocrisy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tell us why, please, Madam.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is hypocrisy. The Muslims in Zepa had no choice. It was not an option for them to surrender their weapons and stay. I told you that I heard with my own ears when they issued calls for Muslims to move with white flags towards Brezova Ravan. They said, "You may not remain here any longer. Go to the territory under the control of Alija Izetbegovic." The buses were already lined up at Boksanica. What they wanted Avdo to do is to surrender his troops, his troops to lay down their weapons, at which point they would become prisoners of war. Avdo could not allow for the troops to be handed over to Mladic and to become prisoners of war. And to separate civilians from the army, well, something would happen to civilians and something else would happen to prisoners of war. Deportation was not contentious. As soon as the attack started, he said, "Let us leave. Let us move out." And this is why I say that this is hypocrisy. Let me tell you, gentlemen, the attacks on Zepa started in 1992. In August of 1992, there was an attack which was repulsed, and in that attack an officer of the Serbian army was killed. They found on him some documents where it said,"Regardless of casualties, you have to reach the Drina by the 20th of September." The messages we received were,"You cannot remain at the border with Serbia. Go to Alija's territory." So it was not an option for us to stay. We could not stay. This is hypocrisy. I don't know what other word to use to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the middle of July of 1995, and I think you've touched on this already, the relationship between the inhabitants of the enclave and UNPROFOR broke down. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. The population did not have a relationship with UNPROFOR. This was something in the hands of legitimate authorities; president of the War Presidency and other people holding such posts. So the population had actually no relationship with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the answer that you just gave, did you say that your husband was also party to a relationship with UNPROFOR? Let me --

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I only ask you that because it didn't come out in the translation.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Avdo had constant contacts with UNPROFOR, even before the attack on Zepa started, and I think that his relationship with them was exceptionally good. He had excellent communication with everybody in UNPROFOR, with commanding officers of UNPROFOR in Zepa. So I really can't tell you anything about bad communication or bad relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look, Madam, at 6D34, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the number, because 6D34 is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am told it is, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. If you have a hard copy, perhaps we can put it on the ELMO. We don't seem to have it, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. We are looking for an unmarked copy. We have found one, I'm glad to say, Your Honour. This can be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I apologise to the Registrar through Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, this is a document dated the 16th of July of 1995. If we go to the bottom, just for a moment, we can see it's from your husband. If we go to the top, sorry, Madam Usher, we can see that it's to a -- urgent to a number of bodies, one of which is the Main Staff of the ABiH. And in particular, I would like you to read the sentence that begins "UNPROFOR." Could you read that out aloud, please?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We are disarming UNPROFOR pursuant to previously given instructions."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea what your husband meant in that communication to his bosses in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I simply know that the weapons that were laid down in 1993 were returned once the attack started, so it may refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have -- perhaps, we could leave that on the ELMO for a moment and put up on e-court 6D30. This, Your Honours, is the actual agreement on disarmament in the military-able population in the enclave of Zepa, dated the 24th of July of 1995, which I'm sure would be introduced into this case in due course by the Prosecution in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'd like you to have a look at paragraph 4, Madam, which I will read out. It says, "All members of UNPROFOR in Zepa shall be immediately released and deblocked. All their weapons and equipment shall be returned to them so that they may mediate in the implementation of the agreement." Assuming that this document is correct in relation to its factual base, did you have any knowledge that the weapons of the UNPROFOR forces in Zepa had been taken and blocked?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that, but it is very difficult for me to speak of something that is taken out of context. I'm sure that there is additional information that could provide a fuller picture to me than just this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now -- well, perhaps I could deal with that and other things in this way: We, and I'm sure this goes for the Prosecution as well, have at our disposal a number of other documents, some of which you mention your husband, were sent to him or were from him at around this period of time. But perhaps we should clarify the following: You, as you have already told us, had moved to a village, firstly. Secondly, you had two young children, and presumably you were not terribly well informed as to precisely what your husband was doing in those critical days in the middle of July of 1995. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, I wasn't able to know all of the details, but what I did know is that he did everything in his power to save the people of Zepa and to save his soldiers. This is something that I was absolutely sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in short, if I was show you further specific documents, it's quite clear that you weren't aware of documents that he was receiving or sending out at this period of time. Quite understandably you weren't aware, I make no criticism of that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the documents, naturally. But as for the information coming in from Sarajevo, yes, we were all interested in that. We knew about what the information -- what information came in from UNPROFOR or from Mladic. We were interested in that and we knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to something which you perhaps do have first-hand knowledge of. When you came down from your mountain retreat, were you aware of any damage being caused to abandoned houses by the fleeing population?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. People didn't have time to think about that. I know what you're thinking of, whether they destroyed their own homes. No, people simply fled. Everybody wanted to get to the centre of Zepa as soon as possible because the evacuation started there. People feared for their lives, and that was the primary concern. People didn't have time to go back to their homes to take basic necessities, let alone do something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps, we could briefly look at 6D29, please. For some reason that microphone has just packed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, Madam, is a document dated the 26th of July of 1995 from a man called David Harland, an UN official, detailing the situation in Zepa. Could we go, please, to -- no, we are at the right part. If we look at ii, it says, "Bosnians, other than men of military age, were coming down from their hamlets in their hills, into the Serb-controlled villages and were waiting to be moved by Serb buses to the confrontation line near Kladanj. Many houses in the hills were burning, apparently torched by departing Bosnians." What do you have to say about that statement?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is so preposterous. When I was leaving, the houses were on fire in areas where the Serb army was already present, in areas from which people had already fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your own physical departure. You were on one of the first buses to leave the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second convoy, on the second bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there a foreign soldier, Ukrainian or French, on that bus with you?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At one point in time a Serb soldier came in, but he didn't travel with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And your bus went to Kladanj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. It went to the separation line and then we went to Kladanj. We started going Kladanj at 4.00 a.m., and we arrived there at 9.00 a.m. We travelled for a very long time in a truck and then on foot. They didn't -- the buses didn't take us to Kladanj, no. They took us to the demarcation line or separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of other buses arriving at wherever you ended up, sometime a day or two later? In other words, were you present when the rest of the civilian population arrived in subsequent bus loads?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present because we rested in Kladanj and then we continued our journey towards other towns that would receive us; and then other people came in to rest in that camp and then continued elsewhere from there. If I understood your question well, I wasn't there to wait for anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You did understand the question, and I'm going move on and I'm going to move to my final topic. And that's this: I began by asking you about your husband, and I want to go back and ask you a little bit more about him. Were you aware that Serbian authorities wanted to speak to your husband about an alleged atrocity that occurred in the Sokolac municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No knowledge of that at all?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know what atrocities you're referring to. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I can make it any plainer. I'll show you some documents in a moment. But there had, in June of 1992, been some form of attack on a Serb convoy going from Pale, in fact, to Zepa. And -- you're applauding. Why are you doing that, Madam?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know what you are referring to, sir. What you are trying to say. Yes, bravo, go ahead. I wish to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What am I referring to?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to a convoy which was on its way to Zepa in 1992 in June. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know quite enough. This was the first attack launched by the Serb army on Zepa, and through my research I was able to establish that this was considered to be one of the greatest sins of Avdo. If I can explain. There was a small barracks, an observation post of the former JNA on Zepa mount. It was called Desetina, and I know it was manned by eight soldiers. It was -- Desetina means squad. Many settlements around Zepa fell in 1992. Terrible stories were circulating around that slaughtered bodies were flowing down the Drina from Visegrad. It was terrible and we knew what happened to those other settlements, and we were expecting the same for us -- to happen to us. On the 4th of June, a convoy set out with 40 vehicles carrying aid to the mountain, aid to the unit on Zepa mount. They went first through some villages near Han Pijesak. They were calling for peace and saying that all they were doing was taking food to their soldiers on the mountain. So they were transporting food. The convoy consisted of 40 vehicles with an ambulance at the back. They travelled through Stoborani and other villages, and people quite understandably realised that it was preposterous to believe that they were carrying only food in those 40 vehicles. And they knew that had they arrived the mountain, nobody would have remained in Zepa, that nothing was organised in Zepa. At the time there was no army there. People were scared. They ran bare-handed to a canyon called Buducim Potok, and they waited for the convoy there. At the helm there was a tank, and people started throwing boulders down blocking the road so that they couldn't pass through. They were rolling big boulders down; however, they didn't stop. They started shooting then they started rolling logs down on the road to block the passage. Some of the cars stopped. There is no reason why this shouldn't be known. One of the logs fell on the road and a tank drove over that log; and since the road was slippery, the tank slid down, which created panic among Serb troops. Many among Serb soldiers committed suicide, or rather caused their own deaths by throwing bombs on -- or hand-grenades on trucks full of weaponry. So this is how they died. The -- those who survived were captured on the following day and were later exchanged for flour. Let me just tell you one more thing. This is something for which Avdo is blamed for. According to some reports that I read in some Serb documents, this was not anything to do with Avdo. This was a struggle by a -- this organised crowd or by the people to defend themselves, to prevent this convoy from reaching this position up on the mountain. Because had they reached that position, they would have killed us all for sure. So this was -- the Serbs must admit that they were -- that the situation was as follows: They were killed by logs and rocks, and they had to leave some of the weapons in the hands of the people of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is some inconsistency in the transcript. I believe that what the witness said is that dead bodies were exchanged for flour. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript from what I could follow of course was that some were captured and later exchanged. Ms. Palic, you need to clear this up for us because it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The captives were exchanged for flour. And the dead bodies, once UNPROFOR arrived, some people came from the Serb side and the whole area was searched and the bodies that -- the bones that were found were handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, I'm not going to go into the rights or wrongs of that incident. It is apparent to you, is it not, that the Serbs took a very dim view of what happened in that creek?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite clearly. But in this case they are blaming the wrong side, because it wasn't the people of Zepa who invited them there to get killed. They should have blamed their commanders who sent them there to Zepa. What did they want there? Why did they attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And there can be but no -- let me rephrase that. Do you accept that your husband was involved in that particular operation that resulted in the deaths of a significant number of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a participant, but he was not a commander at the time because there was no command. There was no organised army at that time in Zepa because the command and the 1st Zepa Battalion were established at a later stage. Only after that did people start joining the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it is right, isn't it, that criminal reports had been filed in relation to this incident and named your husband among quite a number of other people as being involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you be more precise? Criminal reports filed where?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In which case I will show one to the witness, Your Honour. May I have a moment. I am grateful to Mr. Krgovic. 6D33, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a report to the Prosecutor in Sokolac dated the 20th of May of 1994. We look at number 5, and we see your husband's name. And if we go to the second page, at the bottom of that page, we see the word in B/C/S, "Explanation," and then it gives some account of this incident, which I'm not going to ask you to read now, unless you want to, of course.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But this is some sort of criminal report within the Republika Srpska in relation to this particular incident, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you aware that the case is still open, or put another way, it hasn't been closed?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to this case. I heard about this criminal report because I got it in some files that I'm using in the legal suit, or rather, in the process of trying to find the truth about what happened to my husband. I am aware of the existence of this criminal report. Perhaps, I don't have this specific report, but I do know that he was charged under this article of this law. All I have to say is that I can see no point in filing or prosecuting somebody who was trying to defend himself. In fact, what happened there is more that Serbs killed each other because of this fear and panic than that... doing at that time, with stones, it's shameful, we killed them with stones and logs. And they simply went on to list names of people that they knew, and they filed a criminal report against them for defending themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In conclusion, let me make this clear: Nothing could possibly excuse the kidnapping and detention and disappearance of your husband. But what I am suggesting to you is that there were legitimate reasons for Serb authorities wanting to speak to him. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To speak about the events -- about this event in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Madam. The event in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
