utterances.text: Well, there was nothing to speak about. I don't know what kind of conversation you have in mind. Please. As soon as UNPROFOR arrived, the terrain was searched. All the bones, the remains, the mortal remains were handed over. All the prisoners of war were handed over alive, so I can't see what was left to discuss here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else, Your Honour. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that UNPROFOR had control points around Zepa, check-points around Zepa? Is it true?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the centre of the town, could you see these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. In fact, perhaps you could see the one at Brezova Ravan.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: One of these check-points was Boksanica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since you couldn't see these check-points, how could you see the buses, which apparently you saw on the day you heard a voice calling from the hills from Zepa, to leave Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic said that the buses were waiting. I didn't say, or in fact if I did, I have to correct myself, perhaps. Because I was upset, I may have said something which was not correct. I didn't see them, but people who lived up there, near Boksanica, did. Those people, that was the first group of people that came to Zepa to ask what are we going to do? Are we going surrender?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. But you, personally, you have not seen those buses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the voice that you heard, you don't know if it was General Mladic's voice?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure that this was General Mladic's voice, but this was a very resolute voice; and at any rate, he introduced himself as General Mladic. I don't flow if somebody was -- somebody dared to introduce himself as General Mladic. Well, that's a different case then. But even if that person introduced himself as General Mladic, he probably did so with General Mladic's approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is what I thought as well. It was probably, you said "probably" somebody else's voice, but you cannot be sure of this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be sure, of course, that it was Mladic. I can be sure about what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you left because of the shelling at Stitkov Dol [as interpreted], and you said that most of the civilian population followed you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I did not leave because Stitkov Dol was shelled. I said that we left in the night between the 23rd and the 24th --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, I apologize. I have to interrupt you. I'm terribly sorry. I think there was a mistake. My question was the follows: You left Zepa to go to Stitkov Dol because Zepa was shelled?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The civilian population of Zepa followed your family and they left with you to Stitkov Dol; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them, the people living on the left-hand side of the town in relation to the town centre. I don't know what was happening on the right-hand side, but at any rate everybody was fleeing their homes and trying to find a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, when you talked about the right-hand side, and you say that you don't know if the people who were on the right-hand side were evacuated as well, you don't know if they were evacuated afterwards. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were heading, but they all fled their homes. The right-hand side was especially at risk. They were much closer to the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if those people ran away from their houses, where could they have gone? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as usual, into the woods, into the caves, into sheltered areas such as gorges.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know how many people lived on that right side of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said about 2.500 civilians were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've told us that there were 2.500 civilians in Stitkov Dol. Does that also include the civilians that lived on the right-hand side of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's really impossible for me to know all that. I know that there was this huge mass of people there, that people were lying on the meadows, that all the houses and all the outbuildings were crammed full of people. They were kept aside for the women, children, the elderly, for the people who really needed shelter and accommodation. There may have been some people from the right-hand side of Zepa there, too. And there is, in fact, no reason for me to make this distinction, but I do know that this part of town, when we headed out, the people from this area followed me when I headed out because everybody felt that they were safer, that was like a rule of thumb. You were safer with the commander's wife. Wherever the commander's wife, you had to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. Can we therefore conclude that at Stitkov Dol, on that day when you left, that most of the civilian population from the Zepa enclave gathered at Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in the fields, more or less. Well, there were other groups of refugees that -- but this one was from the left-hand side of the town, but there were other groups of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, I feel that we won't be able to understand each other. You say on the one hand that, yes, the civilian population followed you to Stitkov Dol, and then you say that it was the people who lived on the left-hand side. I understand that it was the left-hand side population, or the population which lived on the left-hand side, but can you evaluate, can you tell me how many people approximately lived on the right-hand side of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did say on the right-hand side, I have to apologise. I meant the left-hand side, the villages that were closest to the front-line; Slap, Rubioc, Vratar. They were located to the right of the city centre. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I would like to know is the following: The population that gathered at Stitkov Dol the day you left to Stitkov Dol, was that population that gathered there, was also the population of the entire area of the enclave or only the right-hand side? And can you give us an assessment of the population or of the number of people who lived on the other side of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that when Zepa fell it had at least 8.000 inhabitants, and you can reach all other conclusions if you apply some math.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So the population that followed you that wasn't the major portion of the population, it was the smaller portion of the population because there is a lot of people who didn't follow you. More people did not follow you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is correct. They had no physical links with the area where I lived. The area where I lived and the area -- and the villages around it, those were the people that headed out. The territory of the enclave of Zepa is -- it's scattered. There were places such as Luka and Krusev Dol which were on the other side of the mountain, and they could not have gone with me. I mean they could have, but they didn't. Bioca, Vratar, Slap, and Kula, and other villages on that side did not go with us. Everybody had their own route to follow, but in the final analysis, and this is what we learned during the war, is that everybody was heading in the same direction, towards this mountain.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, this is exactly what I'm trying to establish here. I seemed to understand from your statement that in case of danger the population should gather at Stitkov Dol, and I thought that this meant the entire population. So I am wondering how is it that only 2.500 people gathered at Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all of them were always together.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I will move to another topic. You have stated earlier today on page 8 of the transcript, while talking about a decision from your husband, according to which Zepa should be defended, because if the men of Zepa should surrender they would have had the same plight as Srebrenica. So can you give us the date of the decision when the decision regarding the defence of Srebrenica was taken?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. It's Zepa I'm talking about, so could you tell us when the decision to defend Zepa was taken?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I really don't know the date. The decision was made at the moment when Avdo was told in his talks with the UN that the UN could not protect the people of Zepa. And at that moment, if you as the UN cannot do it, then we will defend ourselves. Avdo's goal was to buy time and to get the United Nations to see what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. We have dealt with this already. I mean what the question referred to was the date, if possible. So move to your next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that on the 15th of July, or do you know if on the 15th of July a meeting of civilian authorities of Zepa took place, so between them and between the Serb military, Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Zepa. The meeting did take place. I don't know whether it was on the 15th of July. It was held at Boksanica at check-point 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know if the civilian authorities were more inclined to suggest an evacuation of the civilian population at the time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was any disagreement between the military and civilian authorities. The only goal that everyone had was to survive. What I do know is that the negotiations at Boksanica, well, you could use any term you wished, but they were held at the territory held by Mladic, and Mladic was talking to people. Hamdija Torlak, one of the negotiators, came to our house and he just lie down, and he was tense for a long time and then he just said,"I had to sign the surrender of Zepa." What kind of negotiation were there, were these then? And how could you talk about any interest the civilian authorities had in the evacuation of Zepa? Well, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, we will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have -- I only need five more minutes, but, in fact, if you wish, Mr. President, we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: We have a few questions, but no longer than more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During -- just before the break, we talked about the authority, the civilian authority's position regarding the evacuation. That evacuation took place, in fact, at a certain point. So during the evacuation, did you see if somebody wanted to stay in Zepa, refusing to leave? Did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anything like that. Nobody could stay. Everybody just moved out. And I have to say this was not an evacuation; this was deportation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that the time of this evacuation or to use a neutral word, transfer, that the UNPROFOR representatives and the Red Cross representatives were there, were in Zepa at the time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was present there, but I didn't see the Red Cross anywhere. Although, it was my husband's view that if the people had to leave Zepa, then they had to leave on UNHCR vehicles, not on vehicles sent by Mladic, and they had to be accompanied by the International Red Cross. I, however, did not see any such vehicles there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you are telling us, and you can confirm, that the UNPROFOR was present when the people were getting on those buses?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was present there. They were in their base, they were not there around the buses, at least I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Fauveau, because the transcript shows the last part of -- and basically the main part of her answer as a question, so that should be corrected. I'm referring to lines 18 and 19. They should be a continuation of her answer, which starts on line 17 of page 53.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I have to ask you the question again, because of the transcript. Can you confirm that the UNPROFOR was present at that place where the people were getting on the buses?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. The buses were lined up in the centre of Zepa, along the main street in Zepa; and perhaps some 150 metres away from this area where the buses were, there was the UNPROFOR base. So UNPROFOR was there, but I was at the head of this column of buses and I did not see. I didn't even look for the UNPROFOR troops. I was just trying to find where Avdo was, and I saw this group of Serb soldiers. But UNPROFOR at that time was still in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that as part of the population that was evacuated in that convoy where you were evacuated, there were able-bodied men as well?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. There were no men of military age. From what I was able to tell, there were women and children there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, do you know Mr. Abdurahman Malkic?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him. He was a witness. He was also in the secret prisoner in Vanakov Mlin in Bijeljina, where my husband was brought in early August 1995. And I met him because he was an important witness who could help me in my search for my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: That person, Mr. Malkic, told you that he had seen your husband in the month of January of 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't say that he had seen him in January 1996. There might be some confusion here. He saw him at the time when he was in prison. Malkic left before Avdo did. In other words, Avdo remained in the secret prison, and Avdo [as interpreted] left in January 1996 when all the prisoners were exchanged in accordance with the Dayton Peace Accords. As soon as I heard about him, I sought him out and I talked to him about what he knew about my husband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 55, line -- line 1 on page 55. That Avdo should be Malkic or Abdurahman Malkic, not Avdo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "Avdo," I mean Avdo Palic. Abdurahman Malkic is a witness who was in the secret prison together with my husband. He is a man who fled from Srebrenica across the Drina and was arrested in Bajina Basta by the Serbian police, and they took him back to the secret prison in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement to the OTP on the 18th of April, 1999, and in that statement you said that you talked to Mr. Malkic as well as Mr. Ramic. Further, you said, further down on the page 8 of the English version: [In English] "They told me that that my husband was still alive. He was being kept as a prisoner in this Detention Centre. He was last seen by these men in January 1996."

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise if I missed that in the statement. I have to say that when the statement was taken in April 1999, it took us from noon until 9.00 p.m. to do it. And I told him this long story, and it was condensed. And in the end we had less pages than actually should have been, and I was opposed to this process, this condensation. This is not true, what it says here. These two prisoners were released in January 1996 when it was agreed that all the prisoners from all sides should be released in accordance with the Dayton Peace Accord. So these two people were released, they were in the secret prison, and Avdo remained there in the secret prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those two people were absolutely certain that in January of 1996, when they left the prison that your husband was still alive in that same prison. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left the prison, the secret prison, before. So in late August, they were transferred to the Batkovic prison where they received visits from the International Red Cross, where all the prisoners were registered. Quite unlike the secret prison where they had been before. So at that time they left him in the secret prison, not in January 1996, which was the date when these people were actually released from their captivity. I would like to be shown this part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. President. 1D177. Mr. President, it is not in the e-court. Can we show -- could the witness be shown the paper copy, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it readily available, Ms. Soljan? THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it would be -- actually, in B/C/S, it would be page 9, second paragraph. This is not the right page. What we see in the e-court system is the old translation. I don't have the new translation, Mr. President. This is why it's not page 9. Could the witness be shown the hard copy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's going to be done now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's page 9, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. So it is correct that Abdurahman Malkic and Sado Ramic saw Avdo in this secret prison when he was brought in. They were together for a while. Abdurahman Malkic and Sado Ramic were transferred in late August - I don't know the exact date - from this secret prison. Avdo remained in the secret prison after they left. The two of them were exchanged in January 1996, when they told me that they had seen Avdo and had been with him in the secret prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that Mr. Abdurahman Malkic became the president of the Srebrenica municipality afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he held a function in the municipality of Srebrenica. I don't know what it was. I met this man once again when he was a witness for my side when I had this proceeding before the international -- before the human rights centre, but I don't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your quest to find your husband, were you sometimes under the impression that the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina - and I'm talking about the authorities of the federation - were not being very responsive?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is the fact that I had to fight on my own. What I got from the federation authorities was sympathy, which really didn't mean much to me, didn't yield any results. And everybody was just saying they couldn't do anything; they were powerless. But I refused to just settle down with this sense that I was powerless, that there was nothing I could do. I think that the position taken by the Sarajevo authorities was, in fact, to a certain extent inferior, but that they had to do more, put in a lot of effort with the international community to insist, to scream and shout everywhere, just as I did. Because we had an officer who was arrested before the eyes of the international community of the UN and yet nobody moved a finger. The UN didn't do anything, and really this is something that I cannot forgive and this is not something that I can justify.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Palic, when you spoke about leaving Zepa, in order to use a neutral term, you said that you left at 7.00 on the 24th. From what transpired later, I assumed that this was 7.00 p.m., because in your statement it is not specified whether it was in the morning or in the evening. So can we agree that this was the 24th of July at 7.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And you said that immediately after that you went to this location from which you later headed towards Kladanj, and that that was at 9.00 a.m., and that was the 25th?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You also said that you were in the first convoy, I think the second bus. Could you please tell me when did the first convoy move before you? You said that there were the wounded and the sick on that convoy.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was in the afternoon. So when we returned to the centre of Zepa from Stitkov Dol, they had already left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Okay. So they also left on the 24th, that's unquestionable?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now I wanted to ask you about leaving Zepa, just one more question. Do you have any knowledge as to when the process ended, if it started on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended on the 27th of July, the last convoy was supposed to move on the 26th in the evening of the 26th, but it was blocked. I know that there were 806 civilians on it and 30 or 40 wounded people. That convoy was blocked and Mladic wanted Avdo to come to the UNPROFOR base in Zepa to surrender the army, the troops. Avdo of course refused to surrender, and at that time he received reports that General Smith was heading to Zepa to arrange, to negotiate about the fate of the troops, and that's what I also heard from Visoko. This convoy spent the night in Zepa, in the morning again they were not evacuated, and then the wounded were told that they would not leave until Avdo has come to talk about the fate of the army. Two of the people who were only slightly injured went to see Avdo, who was at Stitkov Dol, and told him that the remaining civilians and the wounded people were not allowed to go before he arrived. And he said,"Okay. I'm -- you can go back. I'll follow soon after," and indeed that's what he did. According to witness reports, that was at 10.00 a.m., Avdo entered the UN base. They immediately gave the go-ahead, or rather they said that the remaining civilians and the wounded could get on the buses and the convoy moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat for the transcript, 10.00 a.m. on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 27th of July, 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now, let me move on to another topic. Did you see any helicopters landing at Zepa, during the war, of course?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning in 1992, helicopters kept landing and actually flying over my house, flying very low. I knew that these were the helicopters of the former Yugoslav People's Army. They were heading towards this facility, this Desetina facility at Zepa mountain at Ozlovrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Did you see helicopters later?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I saw planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So can you -- are you then saying that in 1993, 1994, and 1995, there were no helicopters landing in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 1993, when Zepa became a protected area, there were many wounded, many people who stepped on a mine, who had their legs amputated in very bad conditions in the hospital in Zepa. And Avdo requested that all the seriously wounded people and all the seriously sick people be transported to Sarajevo or wherever; and then in agreement with the Serb side or Serb army, through the good offices of UNPROFOR, it was agreed that these people would be evacuated by helicopter and this is what happened. I did see those helicopters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Sarapa and Mrs. Palic, please allow a short pause between question and answer because you have been really moving fast, and that's creating problems for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any knowledge that something else was transported in those helicopters? To be more specific military equipment?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you something about Zepa. But this pertains to the pre-war period, until 1992 when the conflict broke out. Was Zepa the seat of the municipality; in other words, was it a municipality or was it part of another municipality?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a municipality until sometime in the 1970s; then it was -- the municipality was dissolved and the areas that gravitated towards the municipality of Hans Pijesak were now part of Han Pijesak, a part of it was now part of Visegrad, and the rest of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So in 1992, Zepa was not a municipality?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. But the territory that managed to defend itself against the attacks by the Serb forces was in fact the territory of the former municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please -- just a moment. At the beginning of the war, in 1992, did Zepa have its hospital?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Was it a health care centre or a hospital?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a health care centre that became a hospital because there was such a large number of wounded and sick people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Was there a court there?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, was there a high school there in 1992 in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In 1992, was there street lightening -- lighting in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: How could you describe the centre? Could you be more specific how many streets? How long were the streets?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the main street. I don't know how long it was really. If you want more specific answers, I don't know if I understood you correctly. But Zepa was an old town, it had its main street, it's the heart of the city, and then there were some other inhabited areas, neighbourhoods closer or further away from the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So those -- those were not those of villages or neighbourhoods were not actually part of Zepa proper?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you describe Zepa as a town, a small town, or a city?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zepa was a small town, in a classical sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Is there re-examination, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, we don't have any further questions for you, which means you're free to go. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and I also wish you a safe journey back home. Our staff will assist you with the necessary arrangements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, documents. Do you have any documents to -- that you wish to tender, Ms. Soljan? None.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand, the Gvero Defence team wishes to tender some documents. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were a number of documents that I put to the witness. 6D29, which was the report by the UN official in relation to the state of affairs at the time, 26th of July. 6D30, which was the Zepa disarmament agreement. 6D31, which was the demilitarisation agreement of two years earlier, of 1993. 6D32, which is the decision -- I beg your pardon, the document in relation to the loan. 6D33, the criminal report. 6D34, which was the document from Colonel Palic, in relation to the disarming of UNPROFOR. And 6D5D7, which was the document, the order of Brigadier General Hadzihasanovic, in relation to matters in February of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Which one of these have not yet been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A number of them have not been translated. 6D32, 6D34, and 6D33 have not yet been translated. The others either have or are in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any objections on the Prosecution side --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or any of the Defence side? So these last three documents mentioned by Mr. Josse, 6D32, 6D33, and 6D34, are being marked for identification pending translation thereof; and then they will be considered admitted. The rest are being admitted, there being no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So next witness. Are we ready? Because this one has got protective measures. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We should be ready to go, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to check the protective measures are pseudonym and face distortion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime, the Prosecution has filed another motion to convert a certain witness, who would be PW-157, from a viva voce witness to a 92 ter witness, and also for protective measures for the protective measures; namely, pseudonym, visual, and voice distortion. If you could possibly come back to us early tomorrow morning on this, so that we can hand down an oral decision. Thank you. For those of you who couldn't follow, I'm referring to Witness number 68. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, please, you are required to enter a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Please read out the text of this solemn declaration and this will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have granted you some protective measures; namely, the use of a pseudonym and also face distortion. That's to protect your identity. I trust that this has already been explained to you. I just want to confirm that this arrangement is to your satisfaction. I haven't heard your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey will go first, and then he will be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. Go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Sir, if could you take a look at this sheet, it's P02397, and could you tell us, is that you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go into private session just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July 1995, were you in the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on July 11th, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: On July 11th, I fled from Srebrenica towards Jaglici. The group consisted of men and civilians. Women and children went towards Potocari; whereas, us, we went through the woods towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you go towards the woods in -- in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska, the Yugoslav army, launched fierce attacks on Srebrenica. They entered Srebrenica and we were forced to flee. As a result, we had to flee from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive orders to go towards Jaglici, or towards the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear any orders. Nobody ordered me anything. There was such a huge panic among women, children, and men, that everything was chaotic. We didn't know who went or fled where. The artillery and shelling attacks were intense. Shells were landing on us, on people, so we had to leave Srebrenica as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you leave Jaglici on -- around the 11th sometime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I arrived in Jaglici on the 12th, and I left Jaglici on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time of day, just roughly, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you leave with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I set out with men. We walked in a column. One behind the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me skip ahead to the morning of the next day, the 13th. Did you surrender at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Yes. Outside of Kravica, there was a large group of men, including myself. We decided to surrender. We had no other option. So we came down to the asphalt road and surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened when you got to the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, we crossed the asphalt road, we were ordered to raise our hands behind our heads, and then we were ordered to lay down our back-packs. Whoever had back-packs had to put them on a pile. We did that. Again, we walked in a column, one behind the other. We were then ordered to hand over money. Whoever had money had to relinquish it. There was a soldier going around, and we gave him our money; and then we crossed the asphalt road and they took us to a large meadow, where there were several torched and destroyed houses. That location was known as Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you first received orders, I think you said to put your hands on your head, can you describe for us who was giving you those orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: One of the Serb soldiers. I don't know whether he was an officer, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe as best you can the -- the uniforms of the soldiers that were ordering you at this point when you had first surrendered? Just as best you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: They had full camouflage uniforms, top and bottom part; some of them had helmets; some had caps; they had flak jackets on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you got to the meadow did you notice any other kinds of soldiers or new descriptions, anything you would add to the descriptions of any soldiers at the meadow when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: The ones I saw, the ones around me, when they took us to the meadow, there were guards around us so that nobody would attempt to flee from my group. All of them had multi-coloured uniforms on then. There was one standing in front of us, most likely an officer. He also had a camouflage, multi-coloured uniform. He had a white T-shirt, short-sleeved one. He had a knife in his hands; and as we were there on the meadow, he kept twisting and -- the knife and turning, playing with it. He had a semi-automatic rifle, and occasionally he fired a bullet into the air whenever there was some commotion. They would send a person or two to get water in bottles. It was very hot and people kept fainting, and they were cooling them down with water. So in order to prevent any commotion among us to prevent us making any noise, he would occasionally fire into the air, and he would yell at us to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know just roughly what time of day you arrived at this meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: It was morning. It was sunny. In the morning, there was fog. And when we decided to surrender, we couldn't see the asphalt road. We just heard them issuing calls to us to surrender and also that we would be safe and that we would be sent wherever we wanted to go. When we descended down to the asphalt road, this was a bit later, the sun came out, and then the rest of the day it was very warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were at that meadow, when you first got there, can you give us any kind of a rough estimate of how many other Muslim men were at that meadow with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, between 1.500 and 2.000, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And was that when you initially got there or did it increase to that size over the day that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: There was a large group with me. We arrived to that location at the meadow, and then later the number grew. After a short period of time, another column arrived. They had also surrendered, and they were taken to the same meadow where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While you were on the meadow did you see any wounded Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I saw a couple of wounded men. They also fainted and they needed to cool them down. The order came for the wounded to be taken to the houses to be placed in shadow, and people who knew them were supposed to escort them there. So they were taken to these houses, and the houses were to my right. I sat there on the meadow facing the asphalt road, and the houses were to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After the wounded were taken to the houses, did you ever see what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. I don't know what happened to them. I just saw one soldier who brought a man from my group, a man who had escorted the wounded. The Serb soldier said that the man from my group had attempted to flee, and he caught up with him and he brought him back to the meadow where I was, next to a tank. What happened then is this: The man who rode in the tank, he kept going in and out of the tank, and there were some other soldiers sitting on the tank or around the tank. This soldier hit him with his palm on his chin, on his face, and the man fell down on his back. All of us watched it. It was taking place some ten metres from us. Another soldier from another group came. A group arrived, and I didn't know who they were. They had different types of uniforms. They had black uniforms with black pants, black T-shirts, boots, I didn't see any insignia on them. So one of those soldiers in black uniform took an automatic rifle with a clip or a drum, approached the soldier, and basically stood over him and fired a burst of fire into his chest; and then he ordered other people to carry him away, some 20 to 30 metres away, and just to drop his body there. That's what they did. They came, picked his body, and threw it on the meadow; and then these people came back to my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who carried the body? Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. While you were at the meadow that day, did you see if anyone allowed to leave, any of the Muslims allowed to leave that group of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: There were some girls, women, and children, among us. Children below the age of 18, say 13, 15, 17 years or so, they were allowed to leave the group. A convoy came, which evacuated civilians from Potocari and took them to Tuzla. They stopped the buses, trucks, and those whom they had separated from the group, who were younger than 18, were put on the buses and sent to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see or hear how your captors were able to separate the people, how they knew who was younger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, one of the soldiers asked, "Whoever is below the age of 18 come out," so some came out. And using his own judgement, he sent back those who, in his view, were not young enough; and whoever looked young enough to him were separated and put on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And while you were at that meadow, did any senior VRS officers come by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Yes. They did. Later on Ratko Mladic came with his entourage. All of them were well-dressed in new uniforms. He addressed us, saying that there was no need for us to be afraid, to worry, that we would be sent to wherever we wanted to go, that we would not be harmed, that we would be sent to our families. He didn't stay there long, perhaps five to ten minutes. I'm not quite sure. Some journalists came, they took pictures of us, they took footage. They didn't stay long either, and then they left from the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "footage," what do you mean when you say the journalists took "footage"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, they recorded us, and they said to us, "We're taking pictures of you. We are filming you so that we can show to the world just how humane we are, that you came to no harm, that you are safe, that you are in a safe location."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time of day did Mladic come by and give the little talk to the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but somewhere at midday. It could have been in the afternoon. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from that -- the transport that you saw that took some women and the people perhaps under 18 away, did you see any other transport or convoys go by your location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I saw the UN APCs which were there near us. I saw soldiers walking by, but they didn't stay there long. They also transported people on trucks, on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say they transported people on buses and trucks, in which direction were those people being transported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: They were taking them towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you make out who those people on the buses were, and trucks were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Naturally, I could. They were all civilians; women, children from Potocari who had gone to Potocari to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain how it came that you finally left that location that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: We were ordered, two buses arrived, and they awaited us on the asphalt road. They made a selection. They didn't get everybody at the same time. This officer came, the one who stood in front of us with a knife, and he said, "You, you, you, come out. Go down to the asphalt road and get on buses." I was among them. He selected me, too. A lot of people came after me until the buses were full. When I got on the bus, I was unable to find a seat. I stood in the aisle, and we were packed so tightly that we almost suffocated. It was extremely warm. We had escorts; the Serb soldiers were on the bus with us. The buses were headed towards Bratunac and Srebrenica. This is how they were turned, and once the buses were full we were taken towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Before getting on the bus, had anyone told you where you were going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: They told us -- that's what I didn't mention. When they were separating us there at the meadow, we didn't know where we were going, and then told us that they would exchange us for their people, the Serbs, that they would take us to Tuzla. That's what I thought. And once we got on the buses, the buses were not turned in the direction of Tuzla. They were turned in the direction of Bratunac, and I found this suspicious. So we actually headed for Bratunac. They drove us there. They didn't drive us far. They took us to those hangars, the depots at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before we get to the hangars at Kravica, let me ask you another question or two. You say there was a -- a selection at this Sandici meadow. Did you -- could you make out what the criteria might have been -- or was from this selection? What the group selected might have had in common, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, they took out fit men, very fit men, strong men. That was their assessment, and I actually agreed with them. So these were mostly the people that they singled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The translation we got was that you "agreed with them." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, I actually don't understand. Could you please clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be a translation issue, but the translation we got is that you agreed with the -- the men that were separating you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I looked around me, and these were indeed very strong and fit men, Younger lads. And they were the ones that were taken out, singled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Had you seen any other -- aside from the women and these -- the younger men that you have spoken about, had you seen anybody, any other groups of men being taken from the meadow that day before your group was taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I saw who was next to me. Some people were taken away as soon as we got to the meadow. There was a man standing next to me whom I knew very well. We both surrendered together. He was the first one to be taken away. The moment we got to the meadow, we were there for maybe 20 minutes, half an hour, he was singled out. He was, however, wearing a beard. He had been a Hodza in Srebrenica. So they took him and they took other people who were bearded. I couldn't see all of them. I didn't see where they took these people, but they never came back. I never saw them again. I only saw the wounded people being singled out, that's what I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know the name of this Hodza that was singled out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I can't recall the name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Aside from individuals being singled out that day, had you ever seen any, you know, larger groups of people either walked away from the -- the area or transported away, prior to you being transported away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, they separated the wounded; the women; the younger people, people below the age of 18; and the girls. They put them on the buses, and the buses left for Tuzla. So the buses with -- they went together with the convoy of women and children that headed out from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's get back to the moment when the bus you were on leaves the Sandici meadow area. Do you remember roughly what time of day that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: That was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you -- you've described two buses. Do you remember if you were on the -- the first one sort of pointing in the direction of Bratunac or the -- the one behind that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: I was on the first bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know that when -- when you went off towards Bratunac, did any other vehicles follow you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: There was another bus behind us. It was also full of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where did your bus go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Well, I got on at the asphalt road, and we headed in the direction of Bratunac. They actually drove us to Kravica, to those hangars there. So the buses took a right turn and took us to an area in front of the those hangars. We didn't travel for a long time. It was just a short drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did both buses go in front of those hangars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Both buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could get 65 ter number 1563 up on the screen. What we're going to do is get a photo and ask you about that photo; and if we have time, we've only got five minutes left, but I'm going to ask you to draw on that photo on this new machine we've got, and I'm sure the usher will show you how this thing works. First of all, looking at this -- at this exhibit, which I mentioned, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Those are the hangars in Kravica where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the usher is going to give you this pen thing, and you can mark right on the screen; and if you make a mistake, we can start over again. Sorry, we may have a transcript issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right. I believe that I see some marking on the right-hand corner of the photograph under this number, so I believe we adopted -- well there is a section, which shows as a mark on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I know what you mean. In the top right corner, under the reference number, there seems to be some handwritten -- can we zoom on that? Let me try and do it myself here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we thought this was a blank one. This is a -- so I apologise. I think this was an exhibit used in Krstic, but we didn't see this little handwritten stuff. We can find out what it is. I think it -- I mean I can read it, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If we have a clean copy, we will use the clean copy, and thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, for pointing that out. It's very illegible, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, this is -- this is our photo, and I don't think it's any problem with what it says on the photo, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has any one of the Defence teams have any problem with this photo? Go ahead. You may proceed. We have three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you could take the pen, could you draw in where the bus you were in stopped at the -- at the hangar, as best you can recall? And you can just press it right on the screen and hopefully it will work. And just draw -- why don't you just draw a little rectangle roughly in the shape of a bus. I know getting the size right is tricky, but just do your best to draw in a little bus rectangle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Yes, I can. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where was the -- the second bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: Behind this one. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If could you put a 1 by the bus you were in, and a -- just a 2 by the bus that was behind you. Just mark a little 1 next to the bus you were in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just a 2 by the other one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want you to just put your pseudonym, which is PW-111. Just put it in that big cornfield to the bottom right. Just put "PW-111" on the screen, so that we know this is your diagram.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: What should I put in? Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. It's your code-name, just PW-111.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just write under that the date, which is I believe -- sorry, I missed the last 1. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the date which should be 6/2/07.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's probably a good place to stop today, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. This will be saved and will subsequently be tendered. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning. Witness, we have to stop here today. We will see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00 when we will continue and hopefully finish with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
